notes: NHTSA 'F-150' covers the mainstream half-ton pickup; Raptor, Lightning (BEV, listed separately as 'F-150 LIGHTNING' from MY2022), and F-150 Heritage are trim/variant names that may appear as separate NHTSA model strings. IMPORTANT OVERLAP: for MY2004 Ford sold BOTH the all-new 11th-gen F-150 and a carryover 10th-gen body badged 'F-150 Heritage'. NHTSA usually files Heritage under 'F-150 HERITAGE', but any 2004 record on the old body belongs with the 10th generation, not the 11th. Platform codes: the 1997 truck is often cited as PN96 (sometimes 'P221' is misapplied to it); P221 is the 2004-2008 truck, P415 the 2009-2014, P552 the 2015-2020, P702 the 2021-present. Sources broadly agree on the 1997/2004/2009/2015/2021 model-year boundaries.

known_issues.description: E4OD 4-speed automatic prone to overheating, torque converter and forward clutch failure, especially when towing.
Dual-tank fuel selector valve and in-tank pump failures causing stalling and no-start.

Spark plug ejection from aluminum cylinder heads on 2-valve modular V8s (4.6L/5.4L). Only about four threads engage the plug in the head, so plugs back out under cylinder pressure and strip the head threads; failure is sudden and requires thread inserts to repair.
Cracked exhaust manifolds and broken manifold studs on Triton V8s producing a cold-start tick.
Fuel pump driver module (frame-mounted) corrodes and fails, causing stalling and no-start.

transmissions: 6R80 6-speed automatic (2009 only on late builds; primarily 12th gen)

known_issues.description: 5.4L 3-valve Triton two-piece spark plugs seize and break off in the cylinder head on removal. Carbon builds in the gap between the plug shell and the head; the porcelain-tipped lower section separates from the upper body during service. Ford reverted to a one-piece plug for 2008.
5.4L 3V variable cam timing phaser rattle and timing chain tensioner/guide wear, producing a cold-start rattle and eventual cam timing codes.
Fuel pump driver module corrosion causing intermittent stall and no-start.

3.5L EcoBoost intercooler condensation: water collects in the air-to-air intercooler during humid/damp highway driving and is ingested on hard acceleration, causing a stumble/misfire and limp mode. Ford's field fix relocated the intercooler air deflector and later revised the intercooler.
3.5L EcoBoost timing chain stretch and cam phaser wear producing cold-start rattle and cam correlation codes on higher-mileage first-generation EcoBoost engines.
Brake master cylinder internal seal leaks allow fluid to migrate into the brake booster, causing loss of front brake circuit function; addressed by Ford recall action on 3.5L EcoBoost trucks.

10R80 10-speed automatic harsh and erratic shifting, jerking/lunging between gears and a clunk on startup; subject of class-action litigation covering MY2017-2020 F-150 and multiple Ford TSBs beginning March 2018.
Gen 3 5.0L Coyote elevated oil consumption and cam phaser rattle on cold start; also reported on 3.5L EcoBoost of the same era.
Brake master cylinder seal failure leaking fluid into the booster with loss of front brake function; recall covering 3.5L EcoBoost trucks.
3.5L EcoBoost variable cam timing phaser rattle on cold start, traced to phaser lock-pin and oil-control wear; multiple Ford TSBs and phaser/chain kit replacements.
10R80 shift quality complaints (harsh 1-2 and downshift clunk) carried over from the previous generation.

notes: Two fleet-only carryover overlaps must be handled explicitly or two unrelated cars will merge. (1) MY2004-2005: the N-body 5th gen continued for fleets as the 'Chevrolet Classic' / 'Malibu Classic' alongside the all-new Epsilon 6th gen; NHTSA files these under 'CLASSIC' or 'MALIBU CLASSIC'. (2) MY2016: the Epsilon II 8th gen continued fleet-only as 'Malibu Limited' alongside the all-new E2XX 9th gen; NHTSA files these under 'MALIBU LIMITED'. Any 2004-2005 or 2016 record carrying those strings belongs to the OLDER generation. Also note the 2008 model year: retail sales were the new 7th gen, while a small fleet run of the 6th gen was sold as 'Malibu Classic'. The Malibu nameplate was dormant 1984-1996 (no MY1984-1996 cars) and ended after MY2025. The 9th gen rides on GM E2XX, not Epsilon II - several secondary sources get this wrong.

known_issues.description: 3.1L V6 lower intake manifold gasket failure. The plastic-framed gasket degrades in contact with Dex-Cool coolant and engine heat, leaking coolant externally and into the crankcase, which destroys bearings if unnoticed.
Column-mounted electric power steering (EPS) motor/torque-sensor failure causing sudden loss of power assist; subject of NHTSA recall action covering Malibu and Malibu Maxx.
3.5L/3.9L V6 intake manifold and coolant sealing leaks; 2.2L Ecotec timing chain and camshaft position correlation faults.

2.4L Ecotec (LAF/LEA) excessive oil consumption. Low-tension oil control rings lose tension and let oil past into the combustion chamber; consumption of roughly a quart per 1,000 miles is common. Repair is replacement of all four piston assemblies. Subject of multiple class actions over the 2010-2015 build window.
2.4L Ecotec timing chain premature wear/stretch, typically traced to the tensioner and upper guide, setting cam/crank correlation codes.
6T40/6T45 6-speed wave plate fracture in the 3-5-reverse clutch, causing loss of 3rd, 5th and reverse.
2.4L eAssist mild-hybrid system battery pack and 12V/battery-cable faults; the eAssist variant was dropped after 2014.
Frequent complaints of hard starting and electrical faults on the 2013 launch year, largely resolved by the heavy 2014 front-structure and interior revision (a facelift, not a new platform).
VT40 CVT loss of forward drive or slipping, commonly with DTC P2714, caused by the clutch regulator valve sticking in the valve body.
1.5L LFV turbo oil consumption, PCV diaphragm failure and intake-valve carbon buildup typical of the direct-injection design.
Missing or improperly torqued start/stop accumulator end cap bolts allowing an oil leak onto hot components (fire risk); NHTSA recall 20V-668.

notes: US model-year boundaries are one year later than the calendar-year figures Wikipedia often quotes (e.g. the XV20 launched in calendar 1996 but is a MY1997 car in the US). Verified US boundaries: XV10 ends MY1996, XV20 = 1997-2001, XV30 = 2002-2006, XV40 = 2007-2011, XV50 = 2012-2017, XV70 = 2018-2024, XV80 = 2025-. The XV50's MY2015 refresh replaced nearly every exterior panel but is a facelift, not a new platform. Camry Solara (1999-2008) and Camry Hybrid are separate NHTSA model strings in some years; the Camry Hybrid shares generation boundaries with the base car except that the XV40-based hybrid ran MY2007-2011. Australian-market Aurion and Japanese Camry generations diverge from the US split from XV40 onward - use the US split.

known_issues.description: Early 1MZ-FE V6 and 5S-FE engines are the leading edge of Toyota's oil gelling (sludge) problem, which became severe on the following generation.

Engine oil gelling (sludge) in the 1MZ-FE V6 and 5S-FE I4: PCV and crankcase ventilation design plus coolant intrusion promote oil coking that blocks oil passages and destroys the engine. Toyota ran a customer support program covering affected 1997-2002 engines for 8 years with no mileage limit.
2AZ-FE cylinder head bolt threads strip in the aluminum block, causing head gasket leaks and coolant loss; Toyota issued a warranty enhancement and revised the block with larger head bolts.
Tail end of the 1MZ-FE oil gelling program (engines built through 2002).
Takata front airbag inflator propellant degradation; large-scale recall coverage across this generation.

2AZ-FE excessive oil consumption caused by undersized oil-return holes beneath the oil control rings, letting oil accumulate and burn. Toyota's Warranty Enhancement Program ZE7 extended coverage to 10 years / 150,000 miles and replaced pistons and rings on engines failing the oil-consumption test.
Unintended acceleration from floor mat pedal entrapment and, separately, sticking accelerator pedal assemblies; the subject of Toyota's 2009-2010 recalls.
Dashboard material degrades and becomes sticky/shiny with heat exposure; Toyota ran a warranty enhancement for affected vehicles.
Torque converter lock-up shudder at light throttle on the 6-speed automatics, addressed by fluid and control software updates.
2AR-FE water pump leaks and, on higher-mileage cars, oil consumption; far less severe than the preceding 2AZ-FE issue.

Denso low-pressure in-tank fuel pump impeller cracks from excessive fuel absorption, deforming and contacting the pump housing; causes rough running, no-start and stalling at speed. Subject of NHTSA recalls 20V-012 and 20V-314.
Low-speed hesitation and harsh engagement complaints on the 8-speed automatic, particularly early builds.

engines: 2.5L A25A-FXS with fifth-generation Toyota Hybrid System (hybrid-only; no non-hybrid or V6 offered)

notes: The Town & Country nameplate has two distinct eras: a woody-trimmed full-size car/wagon (pre-1989) and the minivan (MY1990-2016). NHTSA data from 1996 is entirely minivan. Generation numbering here follows the minivan lineage: AS 1990-1995 (out of the assigned span), NS 1996-2000, RS 2001-2007, RT 2008-2016. The RT generation had a major mid-cycle powertrain change for MY2011 (3.6L Pentastar V6 + 62TE six-speed replacing the 3.3/3.8/4.0L and the 41TE four-speed) alongside a heavy interior/suspension revision - it is still one generation but MY2008-2010 and MY2011-2016 behave as different vehicles for failure analysis and should probably be surfaced separately on the site. The nameplate was retired after MY2016 and replaced by the Chrysler Pacifica for MY2017; the short-wheelbase Chrysler Voyager (1996-2003) is a separate NHTSA model string.

known_issues.description: 41TE / A604 Ultradrive failure: solenoid pack and clutch pack wear producing harsh shifts, limp-in mode (2nd gear only) and complete loss of drive. Highly sensitive to using non-ATF+4 fluid.
Power sliding door latch, cable and motor failures; doors opening in motion or refusing to latch.
3.3L/3.8L V6 head gasket and intake plenum gasket leaks at higher mileage.
41TE 4-speed continues to fail via solenoid pack, input clutch and pump wear; limp-in and loss of forward gears are the characteristic symptoms.
Power sliding door and power liftgate motor/cable failures remain the most-complained-about non-powertrain item.
Instrument cluster and body control module faults causing intermittent gauge dropout and no-start.

3.6L Pentastar left (odd) cylinder head valve seat and guide wear, most often on cylinder 2, causing a tick, misfire and check-engine light. Chrysler revised the head with hardened valve guides and seats in summer 2012 and issued warranty extension X56 / bulletin D-14-12 covering the left cylinder head for 10 years / 150,000 miles.
TIPM-7 (Totally Integrated Power Module) fuel pump relay failure: the internal relay sticks or fails, causing crank-no-start or a stall in motion with loss of power steering and power brake assist.
62TE 6-speed automatic solenoid, VLP (variable line pressure) and torque converter faults causing harsh shifts and limp-in.
Power sliding door and liftgate failures continue; also widely reported seat-track/Stow 'n Go latch complaints.

notes: Two naming traps. (1) 'Rogue Select' (MY2014-2015) is the FIRST-generation S35 body sold as a cheaper companion to the new second generation; NHTSA usually files it as 'ROGUE SELECT', but any 2014-2015 record on the old body belongs with gen 1, not gen 2. (2) 'Rogue Sport' (MY2017-2022) is the global Qashqai (J11), a completely different, smaller vehicle - a separate NHTSA model string that must never be merged into 'ROGUE'. The third generation has a hard mid-generation powertrain break: MY2021 used the 2.5L PR25DD four, MY2022 onward the 1.5L KR15DDT variable-compression three-cylinder turbo; complaint patterns before and after 2022 are not comparable. CVT complaints dominate every generation and are the single most important failure-mode hub for this nameplate.

known_issues.description: JATCO Xtronic CVT overheating, shuddering/judder, hesitation and outright failure. Nissan extended CVT coverage to 10 years / 120,000 miles on MY2008-2010 vehicles as part of its broader 2003-2010 CVT warranty extension.
Fuel level sender failure giving false readings and inaccurate range.
Engine and transmission mount degradation producing driveline vibration at idle.

CVT shuddering, shaking, hesitation and complete failure. A $277.7M class settlement covering MY2014-2018 Rogue (with 2015-2018 Pathfinder and Infiniti QX60) extended CVT assembly, valve body and torque converter coverage from 60 months/60,000 miles to 84 months/84,000 miles, with reimbursement for prior repairs.

Automatic Emergency Braking false activation - the system brakes hard with no obstacle present, frequently over railroad crossings and metal bridge decks. Subject of an NHTSA defect investigation and subsequent Nissan action.
Panoramic sunroof glass shattering and power liftgate strut failures.

generations.mixed_year_note: Both the outgoing and incoming generation were sold in this model year; NHTSA records do not separate them.

transmissions: Xtronic CVT (wider ratio spread than T32)

known_issues.description: The 1.5L VC-Turbo three-cylinder's variable compression mechanism and turbo system are new technology introduced mid-generation for MY2022; early-build complaints center on rough running, coolant/oil consumption and turbo-related faults. Treat MY2021 (2.5L) as a separate powertrain population.
Continued CVT hesitation and shudder complaints, though on a revised unit; a separate class action was filed over MY2019-2020 and later Rogue CVTs.

notes: THE IMPALA NAMEPLATE HAS A GAP: there is no Impala for model years 1997-1999. The RWD B-body 7th generation ended after MY1996 and the FWD W-body 8th generation began with MY2000. Do not bridge 1996 to 2000 - they are also completely different cars (RWD V8 sedan vs FWD V6 sedan). Second trap: the 9th-generation W-body continued as a fleet-only 'Impala Limited' for MY2014-2016 alongside the all-new Epsilon II 10th generation; NHTSA files these as 'IMPALA LIMITED'. Any 2014-2016 record on the W-body belongs with the 9th generation. Impala production ended February 2020, making MY2020 the last.

known_issues.description: LT1 Opti-Spark distributor failure from coolant and moisture intrusion, causing misfire and no-start.

Lower intake manifold gasket failure on the 3.4L and 3.8L V6. The plastic-framed gasket degrades in contact with Dex-Cool coolant, leaking coolant externally and into the oil; often accompanied by upper plenum warping on the 3.8L.

Key can rotate out of the run position under load from a heavy key ring or road impact, shutting off the engine and disabling airbags; covered by GM's 2014 ignition-key recall campaign for W-body cars.
Turn signal / multifunction switch and body control module faults causing inoperative signals and interior lighting.

4T65-E pressure control solenoid failure producing erratic and harsh shifting and slipping; repair requires partial transmission disassembly. Slipping is the single most reported problem on 2006-2008 cars.
3.5L/3.9L intake manifold and coolant sealing leaks carried over from the W-body pushrod V6 family.
Premature front strut and spring failure, and rear axle/spindle rod wear causing uneven tire wear.
eAssist mild-hybrid battery cable and fuse box faults; the eAssist variant was offered only briefly and dropped after MY2015.
6T70/6T75 harsh 1-2 shift and torque converter shudder complaints.
3.6L water pump leaks; on the direct-injection V6, intake valve carbon buildup.

notes: This map is the NORTH AMERICAN Odyssey. The first generation (1995-1998) is a completely different vehicle from everything after: a compact, four-cylinder, swing-door MPV on an Accord platform, not a sliding-door minivan - it must not be merged with gen 2. The Japanese-market Odyssey is a different vehicle line entirely and its generation boundaries do not apply here. The 4th generation's transmission changed mid-cycle (5-speed automatic 2011-2013, 6-speed phased in from 2014 starting with Touring trims), and the 5th generation ran two different transmissions in parallel by trim (ZF 9-speed on lower trims 2018-2019, Honda 10-speed on Touring/Elite, 10-speed on all trims from 2020) - both matter for failure grouping. VCM (Variable Cylinder Management) is the dominant multi-generation failure theme from 2005 onward.

known_issues.description: 4-speed automatic wear at high mileage; the four-cylinder driveline is generally the least trouble-prone Odyssey powertrain.

Automatic transmission failure - the defining defect of this generation. A bearing breaks apart and metal fragments block oil passages, and the second-gear/countershaft area is starved of lubrication, leading to erratic shifting and lockup. Honda recalled MY2002-2004 vehicles (NHTSA 04V-176, roughly 1.1 million units) with an oil-jet kit / oil cooler return line revision, and extended the MY1999-2001 transmission warranty under litigation to 93 months / 109,000 miles. Five-speed units also suffered premature third-gear clutch pack wear.

engines: 3.5L J35A6 / J35A7 V6, with VCM cylinder deactivation on EX-L and Touring

known_issues.description: VCM (Variable Cylinder Management) side effects: running on three cylinders lets oil past the rings on the deactivated bank, causing elevated oil consumption, fouled spark plugs and misfire codes P0301-P0304, and the resulting rough running destroys the active engine mounts. Honda ran a warranty extension for VCM spark plug fouling covering the J35 VCM engines.
Power sliding door and power liftgate actuator failures continue.

engines: 3.5L J35Z8 V6 with VCM standard across the range
transmissions: 6-speed automatic (phased in from 2014, initially Touring / Touring Elite)

known_issues.description: VCM-induced piston ring wear causing oil consumption, fouled plugs and misfires; American Honda issued a warranty extension covering spark plug fouling with DTCs P0301-P0304 on MY2008-2013 vehicles. Broken engine mounts are the common secondary failure.
Power sliding door failures and A/C condenser leaks from road debris.

transmissions: Honda 10-speed automatic (2018-2019 Touring/Elite; all trims from 2020)

known_issues.description: ZF 9HP 9-speed automatic harsh shifting, hesitation and delayed engagement on 2018-2019 lower-trim vans; Honda dropped the 9-speed in favor of its own 10-speed across the range for 2020.
Second-row 'Magic Slide' seat latch may not fully engage, allowing the seat to move in a crash; subject of Honda recall action.
VCM oil consumption and spark plug fouling persist on the J35Y6.

notes: The 1999-2004 'New Edge' restyle is a facelift of SN95, NOT a new generation - the platform is unchanged - but it is worth flagging on the site because the 4.6L 2V head casting (and its spark plug thread problem) changed within the SN95 run. Likewise the 2011 model year is a major mid-generation powertrain break inside S197: the 4.0L V6 / 4.6L 3V V8 / 5-speed transmissions were all replaced by the 3.7L Cyclone V6, 5.0L Coyote V8, MT82 6-speed manual and 6R80 6-speed automatic, so 2005-2010 and 2011-2014 complaint populations are not comparable. The Mustang Mach-E is a separate, unrelated electric crossover filed under its own NHTSA model string and must never be merged into 'MUSTANG'.

generations.platform_code: SN95 / Fox-4 (1999-2004 restyle known as 'New Edge')

known_issues.description: 4.6L 2-valve spark plug thread pullout/blowout. The aluminum heads engage only about four threads, so plugs back out under combustion pressure and strip the head; Ford revised the casting to roughly eight threads for 2004. Repair requires a thread insert kit.
3.8L Essex V6 head gasket failure and intake manifold coolant leaks.
8.8-inch solid rear axle bearing and ring/pinion wear on high-mileage GTs; Cobra IRS bushing and half-shaft wear.
MT82 6-speed manual notchy and grinding shifts, gear clash, 1-2 nibble and high-rpm lockout, worst when cold; Ford issued multiple TSBs revising the fluid, shifter and internals.
4.6L 3V variable cam timing phaser rattle and timing chain tensioner/guide wear producing a cold-start rattle.
4.0L SOHC V6 timing chain guide and tensioner wear (long chain runs to the rear-mounted cam drive), causing rattle and eventual timing failure.
MT82-D4 6-speed manual shift quality complaints (notchiness, grind into 2nd when cold) continue on 2015-2017 cars; Ford revised the unit for 2018.
Gen 3 5.0L Coyote elevated oil consumption and cam phaser rattle on cold start.
5.2L Voodoo flat-plane-crank V8 (GT350) oil consumption and, on early cars, main bearing wear; Ford added an oil cooler and revised specs.
A/C compressor and evaporator failures widely reported on early S550 cars.
Launch-year complaints center on the new all-digital instrument cluster and infotainment software rather than mechanical failures; too new for established systemic defects.

notes: The Outback began as a trim level of the Legacy wagon (badged 'Legacy Outback' through 1999) and did not become a standalone model line in the US until the 4th generation (MY2010), when the US-market Legacy wagon was dropped. NHTSA records for 1996-1999 may appear under LEGACY as well as OUTBACK - check both. The 6th generation runs MY2020-2025; the redesigned, boxier 7th generation (BU) is a MY2026 car, so any 2025 record still belongs to BT. Head gasket failure is the defining multi-generation defect and changes character across generations: the 1996-1999 EJ25D DOHC failed INTERNALLY (combustion gas into the coolant, coolant into the cylinder), while the 2000-2009 EJ251/EJ253 SOHC failed EXTERNALLY (oil and coolant seepage at the gasket edge). Do not describe them as the same failure.

known_issues.description: EJ25D DOHC internal head gasket failure: the multi-layer gasket fails between the cylinder and the coolant jacket, pushing combustion gas into the cooling system and drawing coolant into the cylinder. Typically causes overheating and misfire around 100,000 miles.
4EAT 4-speed automatic duty solenoid C and torque converter clutch faults.

engines: 3.0L EZ30D DOHC H6 (2001-2004, VDC and L.L.Bean)

known_issues.description: EJ251/EJ253 SOHC external head gasket leak: composite gasket degrades at the outer edge and seeps oil and coolant down the block. Subaru's field remedy was a revised gasket plus a cooling-system conditioner additive, with extended coverage on some model years.
Front and rear wheel bearing failure is a common recurring repair.
Catalytic converter efficiency failures (P0420) frequently reported.
EJ253 external head gasket seepage continues; Subaru's TSB coverage on this failure extends through the 2008 model year.
EJ255 turbo failure from oil starvation - the banjo bolt oil supply filter clogs and oil cokes in the turbo center section, destroying the bearings and often sending debris into the engine.

Lineartronic CVT (TR580) chain, valve body and torque converter lock-up faults producing shudder, judder and failure. Subaru extended CVT coverage to 10 years / 100,000 miles on MY2010-2015 Legacy and Outback (up from 5 years / 60,000 miles) with reimbursement for prior repairs, and issued TSB 16-90-13R revising the lock-up torque converter on 2010-2012 cars.
FB25 excessive oil consumption from the low-tension piston ring design; subject of a class-action settlement covering certain FB-engine vehicles.

transmissions: Lineartronic CVT (only transmission offered in the US)

known_issues.description: CVT shudder and failure complaints continue; Subaru subsequently extended CVT coverage for MY2016-2018 vehicles as well.
Parasitic battery drain causing repeated no-start, and widely reported windshield cracking from minimal impact.

engines: 2.4L FA24F turbo H4, 260 hp (XT, Onyx XT, Wilderness)
transmissions: Lineartronic CVT (high-torque variant behind the FA24F)

known_issues.description: Starlink 11.6-inch multimedia unit freezing, rebooting and losing the backup camera display; addressed through repeated software updates.
Denso low-pressure in-tank fuel pump impeller deformation causing rough running and stalling; large cross-manufacturer recall.
Windshield cracking complaints persist from the previous generation.

notes: CRITICAL MY2024 COLLISION: because the UAW strike delayed the third generation, Chevrolet sold TWO different Traverses as 2024 models - the carryover second-generation C1XX vehicle badged '2024 Traverse Limited' (production started January 2024, the sixth and final year of gen 2, mechanically identical to the 2023) and the all-new third-generation '2024 Traverse' with the 2.5L turbo four. NHTSA files the carryover as 'TRAVERSE LIMITED'. Any 2024 record must be routed by that string or by powertrain (3.6L V6 + 9-speed = gen 2; 2.5L turbo I4 + 8-speed = gen 3), or two unrelated vehicles will merge. The Traverse replaced the Uplander/TrailBlazer in Chevrolet's lineup and shares the Lambda and C1XX platforms with the GMC Acadia and Buick Enclave, so defect patterns cross-reference those models.

known_issues.description: 3.6L direct-injection V6 timing chain stretch, setting P0008/P0016/P0017/P0018 cam-crank correlation codes and eventually causing rattle and running problems. Strongly correlated with the long oil-change intervals GM's oil life monitor originally permitted. GM Special Coverage Adjustment #11340C extended coverage for premature timing chain wear on MY2009 vehicles to 10 years / 120,000 miles; later years were not covered.
High-pressure fuel pump and PCV-related oil consumption on the LLT.
Front seat belt tensioner cable can separate from its anchor, leaving the belt unable to restrain an occupant; NHTSA recall covering Lambda-platform crossovers.
Power steering pump and pressure hose leaks causing loss of assist.

engines: 2.0L LTG turbo I4 (RS, FWD only, 2018-2019 only)

known_issues.description: 9T65 9-speed automatic hesitation, harsh 1-2 engagement and shift-quality complaints, plus 'shift to park' message faults from the electronic shifter/park interlock.
3.6L LFY direct-injection intake valve carbon buildup and, at higher mileage, timing chain wear inherited from the LLT/LFX family.

engines: 2.5L LK0 turbocharged I4, 315 hp (V6 dropped entirely)

known_issues.description: The move from a naturally aspirated V6 with a 9-speed to a turbocharged four with an 8-speed is a complete powertrain break; too new for established systemic defects, and complaint rates should not be compared to the prior generation.

generations.mixed_year_note: Both the outgoing and incoming generation were sold in this model year; NHTSA records do not separate them.

notes: US-market split. NHTSA 'EXPLORER' should be treated as the 5-door mainstream SUV only: the 3-door Explorer Sport (1995-2003) and the Explorer Sport Trac pickup (2001-2005, 2007-2010) are separate NHTSA model names and must NOT be merged into these buckets. The 1st gen (UN46, 1991-1994) sits just before the 1996 data window and is included for completeness. Two boundaries are frequently misremembered: the 2nd gen 5-door ENDS at MY2001 (not 2002) while the 3-door Sport continued on the same UN105 body through MY2003; and the 2011 switch to the unibody D4 platform is the single biggest discontinuity in the nameplate's history (body-on-frame truck to car-based crossover) - never merge MY2010 and MY2011 data. The 2025 facelift is a mid-cycle refresh of U625, NOT a new generation, despite heavy interior/electrical rework. The Mercury Mountaineer (1997-2010) is a badge-engineered twin of gens 2-4 and complaint patterns transfer.

known_issues.description: Early expression of the rollover/tire-separation pattern that later became the Firestone crisis; low recommended tire pressure (26 psi) combined with a high center of gravity.

Firestone ATX/Wilderness AT tread-separation failures leading to rollover; 6.5 million tires recalled in 2000 and Ford replaced a further 13 million in 2001. This is the dominant complaint cluster in ODI for these model years and it is a tire/vehicle-dynamics interaction, not a single component fault.

4.0L SOHC V6 timing chain cassette (plastic guide) and tensioner wear on the rear-mounted chain, producing a cold-start rattle and eventual chain jump; repair requires engine removal because the rear cassette is behind the block.
Door lock actuator failure and door-ajar switch corrosion causing interior lights and chime to stay on and battery drain.
5R55S/5R55W solenoid pack and servo bore wear causing harsh or missing shifts, slipping and eventual loss of forward gears; a very high-volume ODI complaint cluster for this generation.
4.0L SOHC V6 rear timing chain cassette failure carried over from the previous generation.
First Explorer with independent rear suspension; rear coil spring and lower control arm bushing wear, and rear differential/axle noise.
4.6L 3-valve Modular V8 variable cam timing (VCT) phaser rattle and cam-phaser-related ticking; also difficult-to-remove two-piece spark plugs that can seize and break in the head.
4.0L SOHC V6 timing chain cassette failure (same rear-cassette design as prior generations).
5R55S solenoid pack and servo bore wear continuing from the third generation.

Power Transfer Unit (PTU) failure on AWD models. The PTU sits adjacent to the catalytic converter, holds only about half a quart of gear oil, and was specified with 'lifetime' fluid and no service interval; heat breaks the fluid down, the internal gears and seals fail, producing a hot/gassy odor, whine, grinding and eventual seizure that can damage the transaxle.

Internal (timing-chain-driven) water pump failure on the 3.5L/3.7L Cyclone V6. The pump is behind the timing cover; when the seal fails, coolant can enter the crankcase and destroy bearings. Weep-hole drip near the alternator or A/C compressor is the early sign. Labor-intensive repair.

Exhaust gas (carbon monoxide) intrusion into the passenger cabin, subject of NHTSA investigations PE16-007 and EA17-002; associated with cracked exhaust manifolds and unsealed body seams in the rear quarter. Most acute on Police Interceptor Utility units with aftermarket upfitting.
Cracked exhaust manifolds producing a ticking noise that mimics a lifter/exhaust leak.
MyFord Touch (MFT) freezing, reboots and unresponsive touchscreen; subject of a class-action settlement.

Rear axle horizontal mounting bolt can fracture under hard acceleration, allowing the driveshaft to disconnect from the rear axle. Because the park pawl acts on the transmission output side, a disconnected driveshaft means the vehicle can roll away when shifted to Park; also causes sudden loss of drive. Multiple recalls covering roughly 250,000-290,000 vehicles.
PCM can intermittently reset while driving, causing loss of drive power, inability to shift into Park, or unintended engagement of Park at speed with possible pawl damage.
Chicago Assembly launch-quality problems produced an unusually dense recall cluster in the first model year, spanning trim, wiring, seat, and rear-view camera issues.

notes: CRITICAL US-vs-global divergence. From the 6th generation onward Honda built a North America-specific Accord that is a different car from the European/Japanese Accord. The Euro/JDM Accord of 2003-2008 (CL) was sold in the US as the ACURA TSX, and the JDM Inspire/Saber shares the NA Accord platform. So NHTSA 'ACCORD' is unambiguously the North American car and the global generation numbering lines up with the US model years listed here. Second caution: Honda's own generation numbering counts the 1994 model as the 5th generation, but the US 5th gen ENDS at MY1997 while global sources often print '1994-1998' (the 6th gen launched in the US as a MY1998 car built from August 1997). Body styles vary within generations (sedan/coupe through 2017, sedan-only from 2018; wagon through 1997). Distributor internal coil and ignition control module failure causing intermittent no-start and stalling.
Power window regulator failure and main relay heat-soak no-start.

Premature automatic transmission failure, worst on the V6 (B7XA/M7ZA). The design starves the 2nd and 3rd gear clutch packs of lubrication, causing overheating, slipping and burnt clutch material; weak differential bearings and the absence of a serviceable filter compound it. Honda extended the powertrain warranty to 93 months/109,000 miles on affected cars.
F23 balance shaft seal leak causing rapid oil loss (the seal can back out of the block); often misdiagnosed as an oil pan leak.
Ignition switch failure causing stalling and no-start (subject of recall action on this era of Honda).

Takata front airbag inflator propellant degradation causing rupture; this generation is in the highest-risk 'Alpha' population for some 2001-2003 Honda inflators.

Subject of a class-action settlement covering 2008-2012 V6 models.
Rear brake pads wear out in roughly 15,000-20,000 miles because the electronic brake distribution calibration applies excessive force to the rear wheels; subject of a class-action settlement.
Unexpected side-curtain airbag deployment traced to a software fault; roughly 300,000 Accords recalled.

Takata inflator recalls cover early model years of this generation.

1.5L turbo (L15) fuel dilution of engine oil in cold climates: incomplete combustion during short trips lets gasoline past the rings into the crankcase, raising oil level and thinning it. Honda Sensing radar/camera false positives causing spurious collision-mitigation braking and lane-keep warnings, often triggered by front grille or windshield conditions.

A/C condenser leaks, a persistent complaint across this generation.

known_issues.description: Internal water pump failure on the 3.5L/3.7L Cyclone V6. The pump is chain-driven behind the timing cover; when the shaft seal fails, coolant enters the crankcase and destroys bearings with little warning. Failures cluster roughly between 80,000 and 150,000 miles and there was no US recall.
Power Transfer Unit and rear drive unit failure on AWD models, presenting as whine, grinding or clunking from the driveline.
Electronic throttle body failure causing 'reduced engine power' limp mode and stalling; addressed by a Ford customer satisfaction program on this era of Duratec V6.
Brake master cylinder seal allows brake fluid to leak into the vacuum booster, reducing braking assist; recalled on 2.0L EcoBoost cars.

2.0L EcoBoost coolant intrusion into the cylinders. The block casting has a narrow coolant passage between cylinders that compromises the head gasket seal, letting coolant enter a cylinder; symptoms are single-cylinder misfire codes (P0301/P0302/P0303), white exhaust smoke and unexplained coolant loss, progressing to washed cylinder walls and engine failure. Ford revised the block casting for roughly mid-2019 production, so later cars are far less affected. The durable repair is a short block or engine replacement.
8F35 8-speed torque converter shudder, harsh or delayed engagement and flare shifts; also reported as a 'clunk' on 1-2 and on reverse engagement.
PTU/rear drive unit failure on AWD models producing whine, grinding and clunk, with costly rear drive unit replacement.
Brake master cylinder seal allows fluid to migrate into the brake booster, reducing braking performance; recalled.

notes: US model years diverge substantially from global production years for this nameplate and this is where most errors happen. Three specific traps: (1) the E110 was delayed in North America - Toyota kept selling the E100 through MY1997 and the E110 arrived only as a MY1998 car (mid-1997 launch), so the US boundary is 1997/1998, not 1995/1996; (2) North America got the E130 body (a US-specific variant of the ninth generation, sold MY2003-2008) while Japan/Europe got the E120 from 2000, so there is a two-year offset; (3) the twelfth generation split by body style - the Corolla HATCHBACK arrived as a MY2019 car on the E210 platform while the MY2019 SEDAN was still the outgoing E170. If NHTSA 'COROLLA' pools hatchback and sedan records, MY2019 is a mixed bucket and needs a VIN/body-style split. Separately, the Corolla iM (2017-2018, a rebadged Scion iM on the E170-family Auris platform), Corolla Cross, Corolla iA/Yaris sedan (a rebadged Mazda2) and Corolla Matrix are distinct NHTSA model names and must not be merged in.

known_issues.description: 4A-FE/7A-FE oil leaks from the valve cover and front crank seal at high mileage; otherwise this generation is regarded as structurally sound with no dominant systemic defect.

1ZZ-FE excessive oil consumption. The early 1ZZ-FE piston has a low-tension oil ring with too few and too small oil-return holes in the ring land; the holes coke over, the ring stops scraping, and the engine burns oil, sometimes a quart per 1,000 miles or worse. Toyota revised the piston design later in the engine's life.

Oil gelling/sludge complaints on some 1ZZ-FE units when extended drain intervals were used; Toyota ran a customer support program covering sludge-related engine damage on several 1990s-2000s engine families.

1ZZ-FE excessive oil consumption from the piston oil-ring/oil-return-hole design, carried over and heavily reported on this generation. Toyota issued Warranty Enhancement Program ZE7 covering 1ZZ-FE oil consumption on these model years with extended coverage.
Engine control module failure causing harsh shifting, check-engine light and stalling; NHTSA recall 10V-292 (2010) covered 1ZZ-FE Corolla and Matrix.

Covered by Toyota's 2009-2010 unintended-acceleration recalls: floor mat pedal entrapment and, separately, CTS-supplied accelerator pedal assemblies that could stick or return slowly due to friction-lever wear.
Electric power steering complaints of wandering, loose on-center feel and darting, subject of NHTSA investigation PE11-016 and Toyota service action on the EPS ECU calibration.
2.4L 2AZ-FE oil consumption from piston ring design on the XRS trim (the same mechanism documented on the Camry/RAV4 2AZ-FE); Toyota ran a warranty enhancement program.

Denso low-pressure in-tank fuel pump impeller can deform from fuel absorption and contact the pump housing, causing the pump to stop and the engine to stall without warning; covered by Toyota's large 2020 fuel pump recall campaign.

Crankshaft position sensor failure causing intermittent stalling and no-restart until cool.
Crankshaft position sensor and ignition coil failures causing stalling and misfire.
Premature catalytic converter and oxygen sensor failure driving check-engine complaints.
Occupant classification system faults disabling the passenger airbag; also Takata inflator recall exposure on later model years.

Steering column intermediate shaft/universal joint coupling can loosen, causing increased steering effort or loss of steering control; recalled.

Turn-key ignition trims were built without an engine immobilizer, allowing the ignition cylinder to be defeated and the car started with a USB connector; drove a nationwide theft surge from 2022 and a Hyundai anti-theft software update campaign.
EPA-mandated 2012 restatement of fuel economy ratings for this generation (not a safety defect, but it generates complaint volume).

Dashboard cracking above the instrument cluster and passenger airbag, widely reported across the GMT800 family.

Dashboard cracking, one of the highest-volume non-safety complaints for this generation.
Power steering pump and hydraulic line leaks causing loss of assist.

Front lower control arm bushing wear and magnetic ride control shock failure on Premier/RST trims.

Dynamic Fuel Management lifter failure on L84 and L87 engines, the successor mechanism to the earlier AFM lifter problem.

Addressed by NHTSA recalls 15V-568 and 17V-224 among others, a knock-sensor detection system software update, and warranty extension to 15 years/150,000 miles. NHTSA assessed Hyundai and Kia a combined $210 million in civil penalties in 2020 over the handling of these recalls.
Panoramic sunroof glass spontaneously shattering; subject of NHTSA investigation and Kia service action.
Electric power steering column motor and torque sensor faults causing sudden loss of assist.

7-speed dual-clutch transmission (1.6T) shudder, hesitation from a stop, and clutch actuator failure.
Non-collision engine compartment fires, subject of NHTSA investigation PE18-019 covering Kia Optima and Sorento and Hyundai Sonata and Santa Fe of this era.

notes: NAMEPLATE DISCONTINUITY WARNING. 'Charger' covers genuinely unrelated vehicles: the 1966-1978 B-body muscle car, the 1981-1987 front-drive L-body subcompact, then a gap from 1988 to 2005, then the modern rear-drive LX sedan from MY2006. The assigned data window (2006-2025) starts at the modern car, so only the LX/LD/STLA generations are mapped here; if any pre-1988 records exist under 'CHARGER' they belong to different vehicles entirely. The Charger is mechanically identical to the Chrysler 300 and, for the LX, the Dodge Magnum wagon - defect data transfers across all three. Within the modern era the LD is a heavily revised LX rather than a clean-sheet car (same basic architecture, updated body, suspension, electronics), but Dodge, FCA and every reference treat 2011 as a new generation and the electrical architecture and transmissions differ enough that they should be separate pages. The 2024+ car is a genuine clean break: new STLA Large platform, EV-first, two-door and four-door bodies.

known_issues.description: Totally Integrated Power Module (TIPM) failure. The internal fuel pump relay welds or fails intermittently, causing no-start, sudden stalling in traffic, and a range of unrelated-looking electrical faults (wipers, horn, fuel pump running with the key off). Replacement modules must be programmed to the VIN. The fuel pump relay failure was subject to major FCA recall and extended-coverage action.

5.7L Hemi MDS (Multi-Displacement System) roller lifter failure and camshaft lobe wear. Sludge and varnish restrict the small oil feed passages to the MDS lifters; the lifter roller seizes and wipes the cam lobe, producing the characteristic 'Hemi tick' and eventual misfire.
2.7L V6 oil sludging and oil pump pickup blockage, aggravated by coolant leaking into the oil through the water crossover; often results in total engine failure.
Front lower control arm bushing and tie rod wear producing clunk and alignment drift.

3.6L Pentastar left cylinder head exhaust valve seat failure/recession causing a cylinder 2 misfire, ticking and loss of power; FCA replaced heads under a warranty extension to 10 years/150,000 miles.
5.7L Hemi MDS lifter collapse and camshaft lobe wear, the same oil-starvation mechanism as the LX generation and still present through the end of production.

845RE/8HP 8-speed torque converter clutch shudder, harsh 1-2 shifts and downshift bump, plus mechatronic/TCM faults; several TSBs issued for cold-start shift quality software. Behavior improved materially in later model years.
Alternator failure causing sudden stalling and in some cases fire; NHTSA recall 14V-634 covered 3.6L Pentastar vehicles including the Charger.
TIPM faults continue on early LD model years with symptoms similar to the LX generation.

notes: OVERLAP WARNING at MY2017. GMC sold two completely different Acadias as 2017 models: the all-new, substantially SMALLER second-generation C1XX Acadia, and a carryover first-generation Lambda car renamed 'Acadia Limited' (production ended 31 March 2017), kept in the range because the downsized new model left a gap above it. Note also that the second generation is genuinely smaller than the first - buyers cross-shopping by year will land on very different vehicles, which is exactly the failure mode of year-based pages. The third generation (MY2024) reverses this and grows again. known_issues.description: 6T70/6T75 3-5-Reverse wave plate fracture. The thin spring-steel wave plate that cushions the 3-5-R clutch apply fatigues and splits, first showing as a flare into 3rd or 5th gear, then loss of reverse and eventually burnt clutch material. GM extended the transmission warranty to 10 years/120,000 miles on affected vehicles.

3.6L V6 timing chain stretch. The original chain design combined with long oil change intervals lets the chains elongate, setting camshaft/crankshaft correlation codes P0008, P0016, P0017, P0018 and P0019, with a rattle on start-up and under acceleration. GM Special Coverage Adjustment 11340 extended timing chain coverage to 10 years/120,000 miles.
LLT direct injection brings high-pressure fuel pump failures and intake valve carbon deposits causing rough idle and misfire.
Power steering pump and pressure hose leaks causing loss of assist and whine.

build_notes: Generation overlap: The MY2017 'Acadia Limited' is this first-generation Lambda vehicle sold alongside the new second generation; MY2017 records span two platforms.

known_issues.description: 'Shift to Park' fault: a micro switch inside the shifter assembly is over-travelled and the button is forced into the switch body, so the vehicle does not register that it is in Park. Contaminated or corroded transmission range sensors and shifter harness connectors produce the same symptom. GM's remedy replaces the shifter assembly and jumper harness.
2.5L LCV four-cylinder oil consumption and low-power complaints; the engine was dropped after 2019 in favor of the 2.0L turbo.

Major mid-generation powertrain change at MY2020: the 2.5L I4 was replaced by the 2.0L LSY turbo and the 6-speed automatic by the 9-speed 9T65, so 2017-2019 and 2020-2023 are distinct failure populations.
Auto stop/start system faults on the 3.6L causing rough restarts and complaints of hesitation.

45RFE/545RFE solenoid pack and torque-converter complaints producing harsh or delayed engagement.
