notes: Simplest map in the batch: exactly ONE generation in the NHTSA span. The Fiesta was absent from the US market for three decades - the original Mk1 was sold here for model years 1978-1980, then nothing until the sixth-generation car arrived for MY2011. It left again after MY2019 (production ended 19 August 2019), so there is no US Fiesta before 2011 or after 2019 in this dataset. Generation-numbering caution: Ford's own global count calls this the sixth generation (Mk6), but many European sources number it Mk7 because they count the 2002 Mk5 facelift separately - use 'sixth generation' and note the alternate. The DPS6 PowerShift transmission is the overwhelming driver of this model's 11,284 complaints; expect the failure-mode hub page to dominate. Also note the Fiesta shares the DPS6 defect with the 2012-2018 Focus, so those two generation pages should cross-link.

engines: 1.6L EcoBoost turbo I4 (197 hp), Fiesta ST 2014-2019

known_issues.description: Dry dual-clutch shudder on take-off, slipping, bucking, hesitation and loss of motive power. Root causes are degradation of the dry clutch friction material and input shaft seal leakage that contaminates the clutch faces. The Vargas v. Ford class action settlement (final approval 5 March 2020) covered 2011-2016 Fiesta and 2012-2016 Focus, with vehicle repurchase and cash remedies; separate later suits allege the defect continued into 2017-2019 Fiestas. This is the defining failure mode of the model in the US.
DPS6 transmission control module failure causing sudden loss of transmission engagement or unintended vehicle movement; NHTSA recall covering 2011-2016 Fiesta.
Door latch pawl spring tab can fracture, letting a door appear latched but open while driving; NHTSA recall.

Clutch actuator and input shaft seal leakage contaminating the dry clutches - the mechanical precursor to the shudder complaints above, and the reason repeated clutch replacements often failed to cure the symptom.

notes: Clean four-generation map with no gaps, but two boundaries carry unusually large mechanical changes. The 2020/2021 break is the sharpest: the XL40 is hybrid-only, so every 2021+ vehicle has a 2.5L four-cylinder and e-CVT while every 2011-2020 vehicle has a V6 and a conventional automatic - no powertrain overlap at all across that line. The mid-generation MY2017 change within XL30 (2GR-FE to 2GR-FKS with D-4S, and 6-speed to 8-speed) is nearly as significant and should be flagged on the generation page. Note also that power sliding door failures recur across three separate generations with different root causes each time, so the failure-mode hub page needs generation-specific detail rather than a single blanket entry. The Sienna replaced the Previa for MY1998; the Previa (1991-1997) is a separate, unrelated mid-engine rear-drive van and should never be merged.

known_issues.description: The 1MZ-FE V6 is part of the Toyota engine family affected by oil gelling - sludge accumulation that blocks oil passages and destroys the engine. Toyota's Oil Gel Policy extended engine coverage to 8 years with no mileage limit for affected owners. This is the defining engine risk for the generation.
Sliding door cable, latch and roller failures causing doors that will not open, will not latch, or bind on the track.

build_notes: Powertrain (mid-generation change): The MY2001 facelift added VVT-i to the 1MZ-FE, raising output from 194 to 210 hp. 1998-2000 and 2001-2003 engines differ mechanically within the generation.

known_issues.description: The rubber oil supply hose feeding the VVT-i controller on the 2GR-FE can degrade and rupture, causing rapid loss of engine oil, possible engine seizure and a fire risk from oil contacting hot exhaust. NHTSA recall; remedy replaces the rubber hose with a revised part.
The spare tire carrier cable can corrode and break, dropping the spare tire onto the roadway; NHTSA recall covering the 2004-2011 Sienna population.
Power sliding door motor and cable failure and doors that fail to latch fully; multiple service actions across the generation.
AWD models used run-flat tires with no spare, producing sustained complaints about tire cost, ride harshness and short tread life.

build_notes: Powertrain (mid-generation change): MY2007 replaced the 3.3L 3MZ-FE with the timing-chain 3.5L 2GR-FE. 2004-2006 and 2007-2010 vehicles have different engine families and different maintenance profiles.

known_issues.description: Sliding door roller bracket and latch failure can allow a door to open while the vehicle is moving; a large NHTSA recall covering the early years of the generation. The recurrence of sliding door failures across three consecutive Sienna generations is a nameplate-level pattern worth its own hub page.
Shift quality complaints - hesitation and harsh downshifts - following the 2017 switch to the 8-speed UA80 automatic.

build_notes: Powertrain (mid-generation change): MY2017 brought a substantial powertrain change: the 2GR-FE was replaced by the 2GR-FKS with D-4S port-plus-direct injection, and the 6-speed automatic by an 8-speed. 2011-2016 and 2017-2020 vehicles should be treated as separate powertrain populations. The 2.7L four-cylinder was offered only for 2011-2012.

engines: 2.5L A25A-FXS Atkinson-cycle I4 hybrid (186 hp engine; 245 hp combined)

known_issues.description: Hybrid-only across every trim - no V6 and no conventional automatic is available. There is zero powertrain overlap with 2011-2020 vehicles, so no V6 or 8-speed failure pattern carries forward. This is the cleanest mechanical break in the model's history.
Too recent for established systemic failure patterns; complaint volume is weighted toward infotainment, driver-assist behaviour and early-build assembly issues rather than powertrain defects.

notes: Six generations, no gaps, but SOURCES DISAGREE ON THE FIFTH/SIXTH BOUNDARY. The English Wikipedia Forester article's summary table shows the fifth generation (SK) running 2019-2025, but Subaru's own press material announcing the 'all-new 2025 Forester' (SL, revealed 16 November 2023, on sale spring 2024) is unambiguous that MY2025 is the sixth generation. I have used Subaru's press release as the more authoritative source: SK = 2019-2024, SL = 2025-present. Second point: Subaru's platform codes shift by production year rather than US model year (SG production began 2002 but the US MY2003 was the first; SH began 2008 for US MY2009; SJ began 2012 for US MY2014 - note the SJ has a two-year offset, so 'Forester SJ 2012' in enthusiast sources is a Japanese-market car). Third: the head gasket and oil consumption failure modes recur across three generations with different mechanisms (EJ25D internal, EJ251/253 external, FB25 ring-design consumption) and must be described per-generation, not blanket-applied.

known_issues.description: The DOHC EJ25D suffers internal head gasket failure allowing coolant into the cylinder, producing overheating, coolant loss and combustion contamination. Distinct mechanism from the later SOHC failures.

The SOHC engines fail differently - external coolant seepage at the head gasket, weeping down the block, often with slow coolant loss and no overheating at first. Subject of a class action settlement; Subaru extended coverage to 8 years / 100,000 miles and specified a cooling system conditioner as part of the remedy.
Front and rear wheel bearing failure producing a growling noise that changes with steering load; a routine failure item across early Foresters.
Rear strut tower and rear quarter panel corrosion in road-salt regions.
External head gasket coolant seepage on the naturally aspirated SOHC engine, same mechanism as the late first generation - slow coolant loss, weeping at the head-to-block joint.

Turbocharger failure from oil starvation, commonly traced to the banjo bolt filter screen in the turbo oil feed line clogging with sludge or debris. Subaru later deleted the screen. Failing turbos frequently send debris into the engine, escalating cost.
Ringland failure on the turbocharged EJ255 - the piston ring land fractures under detonation, producing loss of compression and blow-by. Heavily concentrated on tuned or hard-driven cars.
Continued front and rear wheel bearing failure across the generation.

transmissions: 4EAT 4-speed automatic (no CVT in the US Forester this generation)

known_issues.description: The FB25 introduced for MY2011 consumes oil excessively due to piston ring design, in some cases a quart every 1,000-1,200 miles, with owners reporting oil starvation risk between service intervals. Subject of a class action settlement covering the affected build window; Subaru extended coverage and offered a short-block ring repair.
External head gasket coolant seepage on the carry-over SOHC EJ253 in the first two model years, before the FB25 replaced it.
Takata ammonium-nitrate inflator recall population; rupture risk propelling metal fragments into the cabin.

known_issues.description: Continued excessive oil consumption from FB25 piston ring design; covered by the same class action settlement population and Subaru extended coverage to 8 years / 100,000 miles for affected vehicles.

CVT chain, valve body and torque converter complaints - shudder, hesitation and in some cases loss of drive. Subaru extended CVT warranty coverage to 10 years / 100,000 miles on affected CVT-equipped vehicles of this era.
Windshield cracking from minor or no apparent impact, the subject of owner litigation across several Subaru models of this era.
Takata inflator recall population continues into this generation.

The Lineartronic CVT became the dominant transmission for the first time in the US Forester with this generation, replacing the 4-speed automatic. CVT failure modes do not apply to 2013-and-earlier US Foresters.

engines: 2.5L FB25D direct-injection H4 (182 hp) - the only US engine; no turbo offered
transmissions: Lineartronic CVT (sole transmission; no manual offered)

known_issues.description: Denso low-pressure fuel pump impeller can crack and deform, causing the pump to fail and the engine to stall without warning; NHTSA recall covering MY2019 Subaru vehicles including the Forester.
Continued windshield cracking complaints from minor impacts.
Parasitic 12V battery drain producing repeat no-start conditions, frequently associated with infotainment and telematics modules failing to sleep.

The turbocharged option disappeared entirely for the US market in this generation, and no manual transmission was offered. Every US 2019-2024 Forester is FB25D plus CVT, which makes this generation unusually homogeneous for analysis. A MY2022 facelift added the Wilderness trim.

engines: 2.5L H4 + Toyota-derived series-parallel hybrid system (added during MY2025)

known_issues.description: Launched spring 2024 as a MY2025 vehicle; too recent for any established systemic failure pattern. The hybrid variant arrived roughly a year after the combustion model and is a genuinely new powertrain for the nameplate.

Some references, including the English Wikipedia summary table, extend the fifth generation (SK) through 2025 and would place this generation's start later. Subaru's own press material announcing the 'all-new 2025 Forester' establishes MY2025 as the sixth generation; that reading is used here.

Body-style variants to watch in NHTSA data: Escalade ESV (long wheelbase, MY2003+), Escalade EXT (pickup, MY2002-2013), Escalade Hybrid (MY2009-2013), and Escalade-V (supercharged, MY2023+) - NHTSA may or may not file these under 'ESCALADE'. Separately, the all-electric Escalade IQ launched for MY2025 as a distinct nameplate on a different platform; if it appears under 'ESCALADE' it must be split out. The fifth generation's introduction of independent rear suspension (2021) is a chassis change large enough that suspension complaint patterns do not carry across the 2020/2021 line.

known_issues.description: 4L60-E 4-speed automatic failure - slipping, loss of reverse and 3-4 clutch pack wear, the characteristic GM truck automatic failure of the era.

A rushed two-year response to the Lincoln Navigator, essentially a rebadged GMC Yukon Denali with minimal Cadillac-specific engineering. Low production volume means small complaint counts; interpret rates rather than totals.

known_issues.description: Gauge stepper motor failure causing the speedometer, fuel, oil pressure and temperature gauges to stick, read inaccurately or die. GM issued special coverage extending the warranty on affected clusters. Among the highest-volume complaints of this generation and shared across the GMT800 truck family.
4L60-E and 4L65-E automatic failure under the 6.0L LQ9's torque - slipping, harsh engagement and clutch pack wear.
Intermediate steering shaft wear producing a clunk or knock felt through the wheel over bumps and during low-speed turns; a chronic GMT800 complaint.
Wheel speed sensor and ABS control module faults causing false ABS activation at low speed and extended stopping distances.

engines: 6.2L L94 V8 with Active Fuel Management (403 hp), 2010-2014
6.0L LZ1 V8 Two-Mode Hybrid (332 hp), Escalade Hybrid 2009-2013

Note the pre-AFM L92 (2007-2009) does not share this failure mode.
Dashboard top surface cracks and splits, typically radiating from the passenger airbag seam. Extremely widely reported across the generation; GM never issued a recall, treating it as cosmetic.
GM full-size trucks and SUVs of this generation are part of the Takata inflator recall population.
6L80 torque converter shudder and harsh 1-2 shifts, commonly traced to torque converter clutch material degradation and fluid condition.
Fuel level sender failure producing an erratic or stuck fuel gauge, a shared GM full-size truck complaint of the era.

engines: 6.2L L86 EcoTec3 V8 with Active Fuel Management (420 hp)

known_issues.description: Torque converter shudder and harsh, clunking shifts on the 8L90, traced to degradation of the factory Dexron VI fluid interacting with the torque converter clutch. GM's service remedy was a full fluid flush and refill with Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP. Subject of class action litigation across GM's 8-speed range.
L86 AFM valve lifter collapse and excessive oil consumption, same mechanism as the prior generation's L94 - misfire, ticking and potential camshaft damage.
Electric power steering assist can be lost momentarily, particularly at low speed, increasing steering effort without warning; NHTSA recall on affected early vehicles.
Dashboard cracking continued to be reported into the early years of this generation.

build_notes: Powertrain (mid-generation change): Three different transmissions across six model years - 6-speed for 2015, 8-speed for 2016-2017, 10-speed for 2018-2020. Transmission complaints cannot be attributed to the generation as a whole and must be segmented by model year.

engines: 6.2L L87 EcoTec3 V8 with Dynamic Fuel Management (420 hp)
3.0L LM2 / LZ0 Duramax turbodiesel I6 (277-305 hp), 2021-2024

known_issues.description: Connecting rod bearing failure causing engine knock, seizure and complete loss of propulsion while driving. GM's investigation identified two root causes: sediment contamination in the crankshaft oil galleries and connecting rods, and crankshafts produced out of dimensional specification with inadequate surface finish. NHTSA recall 25V-274 (GM N252494000) covers roughly 878,000 vehicles including about 79,747 Escalades. The remedy is inspection with engine repair or replacement, or a switch to higher-viscosity oil for vehicles that pass. MY2025 vehicles are excluded because crankshaft and connecting rod manufacturing improvements were implemented on or before 1 June 2024.
Independent rear suspension replaced the live axle for this generation, a fundamental chassis change. Rear suspension and ride-quality complaint patterns from 2015-2020 vehicles do not carry forward.
Complaints centred on the 38-inch curved OLED display cluster - blanking, freezing and reboot behaviour - in the early years of the generation.

build_notes: Powertrain (mid-generation change): The 3.0L Duramax diesel was dropped for MY2025 alongside the facelift that introduced a 55-inch curved display. Diesel-specific failure modes apply only to 2021-2024 vehicles.

Contiguous, no gaps: 2006-2012, then 2013-2020. Production ended July 2020; MY2020 is the last. known_issues.description: Electric power-assisted steering (EPAS) sudden loss of assist. Conformal-coat contamination and ribbon-cable pin misalignment inside the steering gear motor cause loss of the motor position sensor signal, dropping assist without warning. NHTSA recall 15V-340 / Ford 15S18 covered ~394,000 vehicles built Sep 2010-Feb 2012; NHTSA PE14-030 had earlier examined 2010 Fusion EPAS complaints.
6F35 six-speed automatic harsh/delayed engagement, shudder and internal failure after the 2010 changeover from the Aisin 5-speed.
Electronic throttle body failure on the Duratec V6 producing wrench-light limp mode and stalling.

known_issues.description: Localized cylinder-head overheating and cracking under low-coolant conditions; cracked head vents oil onto the hot exhaust manifold, causing under-hood and while-driving fires. Coolant intrusion into the combustion chambers through the cylinder head / block interface. Symptoms are unexplained coolant loss, white exhaust smoke, misfires and eventual bearing or cylinder damage; the field remedy is short-block replacement.

Door latch pawl spring tab fractures, allowing a door to appear closed but open while driving. Recall lineage 15V-246, 16V-643, 17V-210, with 20S30 issued as a re-repair after the first fixes failed; all four latches replaced.

Steering wheel retaining bolt may loosen and allow the steering wheel to detach from the column. NHTSA recall 18V-155.

VQ35DE timing chain guide and tensioner wear producing cold-start rattle and, if ignored, chain jump. Subject of the Falco v. Nissan North America timing-chain class settlement.
SkyView / panoramic glass roof water leaks into the headliner and A-pillar.

VQ35DE timing chain wear (Falco v. Nissan settlement) and oil consumption.
