known_issues.description: Failure of the Honda 5-speed automatic — slipping, then complete disengagement without warning, often stranding the vehicle. Reported around 120,000 miles on 2001 and 2003 vehicles and around 80,000 miles on 2004. Part of the broader Honda/Acura V6 5-speed automatic durability problem of the era; repairs typically exceed $4,000.
known_issues.affected_years: 2001-2006, with 2001, 2003 and 2004 the most heavily reported

engines: 3.7L J37A1 SOHC V6, 300 hp, with Variable Cylinder Management

known_issues.description: The cylinder-deactivation system causes excessive oil consumption as oil passes the rings on deactivated cylinders; the consumed oil fouls spark plugs, producing misfires and a check-engine light. Secondary effects include repeated engine/motor mount failure from the vibration of running on three cylinders, and torque converter damage. Owners report stalling or lurching under light acceleration in the 35-45 mph range where VCM cycles.
known_issues.affected_years: 2007-2013, with 2010-2011 the most heavily reported (2010 owners reported averaging roughly $6,800 to remedy)

known_issues.description: Harsh and erratic shifting, hesitation and delayed engagement in the first years of the ZF 9HP application, addressed through successive transmission control software updates. 2016 is the problem year; by 2017-2020 most calibration fixes were in place.
VCM-driven oil consumption and spark plug fouling continue from the previous generation, though better understood and more often mitigated by owners in later model years.

notes: CONTESTED BOUNDARY — B6 to B7. The B7 launched in the US in spring 2005 and Audi marketed early cars as '2005.5', with some sources (AudiWorld's US press launch coverage, Nick's Car Blog) describing the B7 range as '2005.5-2008' while CarBuzz and most US model-year references list B6 = 2002-2005 and B7 = 2006-2008. I have used the CarBuzz/US-model-year split (B6 through 2005, B7 from 2006) because it is the one that matches how the cars are titled and how NHTSA keys model years, but MY2005 records may contain a minority of early B7 cars — flag this on both generation pages rather than silently absorbing it. Other notes: the B7 is technically a heavy facelift of the B6's 8E body, but it is universally treated as its own generation (new engines, new front structure, new suspension geometry) and should be a separate page. The A4 Cabriolet lagged the sedan — B7 Cabriolet production continued into 2009. NAMEPLATE END: the A4 was discontinued after MY2025 in the US and replaced by the four-door A5 (B10) for MY2026, so 2025 is the final A4 model year. Related NHTSA model strings that are NOT the mainstream A4 and should be routed elsewhere: 'A4 ALLROAD' (2017-2025), 'S4', 'RS4'. Generations are contiguous with no gaps.

known_issues.description: Oil coking and sludge formation in the 1.8T, concentrated at the turbocharger oil feed and in the sump, leading to oil starvation and turbo or bearing failure. Driven by small sump capacity, high turbo heat soak and long service intervals. Audi extended engine coverage on 1.8T-engined cars of this era in response.
Coil pack failures on the 1.8T producing misfires and limp mode; the subject of large-scale replacement campaigns across VW/Audi 1.8T applications.
Wear of the multi-link front control arm ('thrust arm') bushings, producing clunking, wandering and uneven tire wear; a defining B5 maintenance failure.

Failure of the multitronic continuously variable transmission: jerky acceleration, slipping under load, unusual noises and eventual loss of drive, typically emerging at roughly 60,000-95,000 miles. Failures involve both the clutch pack/chain assembly and the transmission control unit. Widely regarded as the defining B6 defect.
The 1.8T oil sludge/oil starvation problem carries into the B6; Audi's extended engine coverage for sludge spans 1.8T engines through roughly 2005.

known_issues.component: Engine — high pressure fuel pump cam follower
known_issues.description: The bucket-style cam follower that rides between the intake camshaft lobe and the mechanical high pressure fuel pump wears through and can be punctured, after which the pump plunger contacts and destroys the camshaft lobe, and metal debris enters the oil. Symptoms are power loss, rough running and a check-engine light. The follower is a wear item that owners must inspect periodically; the defining B7 2.0T FSI failure.
Hydraulic timing chain tensioner wear on the FSI engines, permitting chain slack and, in the worst case, timing jump.
Direct injection means no fuel washes the intake valves, so carbon accumulates and causes misfires, rough idle and power loss; requires periodic walnut-blasting.

generations.platform_code: B8 / Typ 8K (MLB); B8.5 facelift from MY2013

known_issues.description: The early EA888 2.0T uses a piston design with 21 mm wrist pins and a ring pack that fails to control oil, producing consumption reported at over one quart per 1,000 miles. Audi initially replaced pistons and rings under warranty, later offering a revised crankcase breather element plus software. Subject of a class action settlement; the revised piston/ring kit is the durable fix.
known_issues.affected_years: 2009-2012 (2.0T); corrected on the Gen3 engine from 2013

known_issues.description: The hydraulic timing chain tensioner is poorly designed and commonly fails shortly after the warranty period, allowing the chain to go slack and jump a tooth on the camshaft, causing valve-to-piston contact and engine failure. Subject of a US class action filed by plaintiffs across 17 states; Audi revised the tensioner design.
The plastic water pump and integrated thermostat housing crack and leak coolant, a routine failure on this engine family.
Carbon accumulation on the intake valves of the direct-injected 2.0T causing misfires, rough idle and lost power.

known_issues.description: The integrated plastic water pump and thermostat module remains a recurring coolant leak point on the EA888, carried over from the B8.
Carbon accumulation on intake valves persists on the direct-injected engine, though the Gen3B's addition of port injection in some tunes reduces severity relative to the B8.

notes: Single-generation nameplate; no generation-boundary ambiguity. Built on GM's Delta platform (shared with Chevrolet Cobalt, Pontiac G5, Saturn Ion), so its failure patterns overlap those cars closely — worth cross-linking on the site. The HHR Panel (no rear side glass, 2007-2011) and HHR SS (2008-2010) are trims, not separate generations. Production ended May 2011; MY2011 was a partial year, so MY2011 complaint counts are naturally low.

engines: 2.2L Ecotec LAP I4 with VVT (155 hp, 2009-2011)
2.0L turbocharged Ecotec LNF I4 (260 hp, SS only, 2008-2010)

known_issues.description: Ignition switch detent torque too low: weight on the key ring or a jarring road event can move the switch out of 'Run', shutting off the engine and with it power steering assist, power brake assist and airbag deployment. Covered by GM's 2014 ignition-switch recall campaign, initially for 2006-2007 cars and later expanded to the full 2006-2011 HHR range.

Loss of electric power steering assist from failure of the steering column assist motor/torque sensor circuit; steering reverts to manual effort. GM recalled a subset of 2009-2010 HHR under its 2014 power-steering campaign (the same defect family as the Cobalt/G5/Ion EPS recalls).

Plastic timing chain guides and the hydraulic tensioner degrade, producing cold-start rattle from the passenger side of the engine and chain slack. The Ecotec is an interference design, so a jumped or broken chain causes valve-to-piston contact.
Excessive oil consumption between changes on 2.4L Ecotec engines, attributed to piston ring/PCV system design; GM issued a technical service bulletin covering 2010-2013 2.4L vehicles.

notes: Single-generation nameplate (2003-2007), replacing the Saturn S-Series and replaced by the Astra. Same GM Delta platform as the Chevrolet Cobalt/HHR and Pontiac G5, so defect patterns are shared. Body styles: 4-door sedan and 'Quad Coupe' with rear-hinged half doors — trims, not generations. Transmission sourcing in 2003-2004 is the one soft spot in the record: the VTi CVT is well documented as the 2003-2004 automatic, while some references additionally list an Aisin 5-speed automatic for those years; the 4T45-E 4-speed automatic is firmly established from 2005 onward.

engines: 2.0L supercharged Ecotec LSJ I4 (205 hp, Red Line, 2004-2007)

known_issues.description: GM's VTi continuously variable transmission suffered very high failure rates — slipping and shudder progressing to total loss of drive. GM halted VTi production in January 2004 and dropped it for MY2005; a class action produced a settlement and extended warranty coverage.

Same low-detent-torque ignition switch as the Cobalt/HHR: key-ring weight or a jolt can rotate the switch out of 'Run', killing the engine and disabling power steering assist, power brake assist and the airbags. All 2003-2007 Ions were included in GM's February 2014 recall expansion.

Column-mounted electric power steering assist motor/control circuit fails, causing sudden loss of steering assist (steering remains mechanical but effort rises sharply). GM recalled all MY2004-2007 Ions under its 2014 power-steering campaign after an extended delay.

notes: Single-generation nameplate, MY2004-2007. It is not a clean-sheet vehicle: it is a heavily revised second-generation Windstar (Ford spent roughly $600M on the update, targeting driveline reliability) and was renamed Freestar for 2004. The Mercury Monterey (2004-2007) is the badge-engineered twin and appears as a separate NHTSA model — do not merge it into the Freestar page, but do cross-link, since it shares the torque converter recall. No direct successor: Ford exited the minivan segment in North America, with the Taurus X and Flex covering the three-row role. Engine availability varied by trim and year (3.9L base, 4.2L on upper trims and eventually standard), so treat engine-specific failure grouping by VIN/trim rather than by model year alone.

known_issues.description: Torque converter output shaft splines strip, causing sudden and complete loss of motive power with no warning while driving. NHTSA ODI logged 227 owner complaints of sudden power loss, 124 attributed to spline stripping; Ford recalled roughly 205,896 MY2004-2005 Freestar and Mercury Monterey vans in 2012 (Ford campaign 11S25, NHTSA 12V-006) and replaced the torque converter.
known_issues.affected_years: 2004-2005 (recall); 2006-2007 vans report similar failures without a recall

known_issues.description: Broader transmission durability complaints across the run — slipping, harsh engagement and failure — continuing the driveline reputation the Windstar redesign was meant to fix.

notes: All years in the NHTSA span are body-on-frame Ford Panther platform cars with the 4.6L 2-valve SOHC modular V8 — the split is by chassis revision, not by drivetrain. SOURCE DISAGREEMENT: Wikipedia's Grand Marquis article treats 1998-2002 and 2003-2011 as separate generations, while some references (and Wikipedia's own Crown Victoria article) treat 1998-2011 as one long generation with a 2003 mid-cycle chassis update. I have used the 1998-2002 / 2003-2011 split because 2003 brought a genuinely different chassis (fully boxed hydroformed frame, rack-and-pinion steering replacing recirculating ball, redesigned front and rear suspension and brakes), which meets the platform-change test rather than the facelift test. If the site later prefers fewer pages, 1998-2011 can be merged, but 1992-1997 must stay separate. Production ended 4 January 2011 at St. Thomas Assembly, so MY2011 is a short year. Sibling cars sharing these defects: Ford Crown Victoria and Lincoln Town Car.

known_issues.description: The plastic/composite intake manifold on the 4.6L 2-valve V8 develops fatigue cracks at the coolant crossover duct (splits across the front, behind the alternator), dumping coolant and risking overheating. Ford's formal recall (01M02) covered only police/fleet Crown Victorias; a December 2005 class-action settlement covered consumer 1996-2001 Grand Marquis, Town Car and Crown Victoria owners with reimbursement of about $735. Manifolds with an aluminum crossover superseded the all-plastic part from roughly 2002.
On air-suspension-equipped cars, rear air springs and the compressor leak and fail, leaving the car sagging at the rear; a common conversion-to-coil repair.

engines: 4.6L 2-valve SOHC Modular V8 (200-235 hp with dual exhaust/Handling Package)

known_issues.description: Same 4.6L 2-valve composite intake manifold coolant-crossover cracking as the previous generation; the 2005 class-action settlement covered 1996-2001 model years, and the redesigned manifold with an aluminum crossover arrived around 2002.
Air spring and compressor leaks on air-suspension-equipped cars produce rear-end sag and compressor burnout.
Rear air springs and compressor leak and fail on air-suspension-equipped cars, causing rear sag and compressor overrun.

The rack-and-pinion steering introduced for 2003 draws leak and looseness complaints not applicable to the earlier recirculating-ball cars — a useful discriminator between the 1998-2002 and 2003-2011 pages.

notes: Full-size body-on-frame SUV, Ford Expedition-based throughout. The extended-wheelbase Navigator L (2007+, chassis U418; later 'Navigator L' on U554/U718) is the same generation as the standard-wheelbase truck and should not be split out. Two mid-generation powertrain changes matter more than any facelift: (1) within the 3rd generation, the 5.4L V8 was replaced by the 3.5L twin-turbo EcoBoost V6 for MY2015, and the 6HP26 transmission gave way to the 6R80 for MY2009 — so 2007-2008, 2009-2014 and 2015-2017 behave like three different trucks mechanically; (2) the 2nd generation switched from the 4R100 to the ZF 6HP26 and from the DOHC InTech V8 to the 3-valve Triton for 2005-2006. The 5th generation (2025+) is very new and has little complaint history yet.

engines: 5.4L InTech DOHC 32-valve V8 (300 hp, from mid-1999)

known_issues.description: Rear (and on 4x4 models, front) air springs leak and the compressor burns out from over-cycling; symptoms are a sagging or squatting rear end, ride-height faults and nose-dive under braking. Height sensors and control module electrical faults are secondary causes.

The 2-valve Triton aluminum heads have too few spark plug thread engagements; plugs (commonly #2/#3/#4) work loose and eject from the head under compression, typically at 60,000-100,000 miles, stripping the threads. Ford revised the head design for 2003.
Air spring leaks, compressor failure and height-sensor faults continue; complaint volume is highest around MY2004.
The 3-valve Triton used a two-piece spark plug whose lower porcelain/shell section seizes in the head and breaks off during removal, turning a routine plug change into head-removal-level work.
Cam phaser rattle at cold start and under light load, and timing chain tensioner/guide wear, on the 3-valve 5.4L; aggravated by low or degraded oil.

Two-piece spark plugs seize and break off in the aluminum heads on removal; Ford returned to one-piece plugs around the 2008-2009 build change, so the problem is concentrated in the earlier years of this generation.
Cam phaser rattle, phaser lock-up and timing chain tensioner/guide wear on the 3-valve 5.4L, producing cold-start rattle and, if ignored, chain jump.
Load-leveling air suspension continues to leak at the air springs and to overwork the compressor across this generation.

Harsh or erratic shifting, downshift clunk and torque converter shudder are widely reported across Ford's 10R80 application base in the earlier years of this transmission; symptoms are typically addressed by TCM recalibration, with hardware repair in worse cases.

The angle (bevel) gear unit and its splined coupling to the propshaft wear and seize, a well-known P2 AWD service item causing driveline noise, vibration and loss of rear drive; often traced to inadequate lubrication/fluid service.

known_issues.description: BECM failure inside the 400V pack triggers 'Hybrid System Failure' warnings and severely reduced power ('turtle mode'); repair requires high-voltage-certified service of the pack.

Recall for a possible short circuit within a high-voltage battery module when the pack is fully charged and the vehicle is parked, with fire risk; remedy is module inspection/replacement plus monitoring software.
Recall R10100: the low-pressure fuel pump can blow its 15-amp fuse and stop, stalling the engine while driving; remedy was a 20-amp fuse.

notes: NHTSA records may appear under RX, RX 300, RX 330, RX 350, RX 400H, RX 450H, RX 350L etc.; all of these are trim/powertrain designations within the five generations below and should be folded into the generation pages. SOURCE DISAGREEMENT resolved: Wikipedia's XU30 table ends the second generation at 2008, but the US RX 350 was sold as a MY2009 vehicle — Lexus's own VVT-i oil line campaign covers MY2007-2009 RX 350, and third-generation US sales began in February 2009 as MY2010 cars. I therefore use 2004-2009 for generation 2 and 2010-2015 for generation 3. Within generation 2 the powertrain changes matter: RX 330 (3.3L 3MZ-FE) 2004-2006, RX 400h hybrid 2006-2008, RX 350 (3.5L 2GR-FE) 2007-2009. The three-row RX 350L/450hL (2018-2022) is a body variant of generation 4, not a separate generation.

known_issues.description: The 1MZ-FE V6 is central to Toyota's oil-gelling episode: sludge accumulates in the crankcase and under the valve covers, starving oil passages and in bad cases destroying the engine. Toyota handled it through a special policy adjustment giving up to eight years of coverage rather than a recall, and a later class settlement covered roughly 3.5 million 1997-2002 Toyota/Lexus vehicles including the RX 300.
Harsh or delayed engagement, slipping and outright failure of the 4-speed automatic are among the most common owner complaints for this generation.

The rubber section of the VVT-i actuator oil supply hose degrades and ruptures, causing rapid oil loss, abnormal engine noise, oil pressure warning and cam timing codes (e.g. P0024) that can end in engine failure. Lexus ran a Limited Service Campaign replacing the hose with an all-metal part, covering roughly 374,000 vehicles including MY2007-2009 RX 350.

Dashboards crack and turn sticky/shiny/melted under heat and humidity. Lexus ran a Warranty Enhancement Program (ZLD) covering MY2004-2006 RX 330 and MY2007-2009 RX 350, with reimbursement for prior out-of-pocket replacements of roughly $1,500.

Included in Toyota/Lexus's floor mat pedal entrapment recall campaign, where an unsecured or incorrect all-weather mat can trap the accelerator pedal; remedy involved pedal reshaping, mat replacement and brake-override software.

Denso low-pressure fuel pump impellers can deform and bind, causing rough running, no-start and engine stall while driving; part of the large multi-brand Denso fuel pump recall covering roughly MY2018-2020 vehicles.

engines: 2.4L turbo hybrid with rear eAxle (RX 500h F Sport Performance, 366 hp combined)

notes: IMPORTANT GROUPING HAZARD: the G35 nameplate spans two different platforms and the body styles changed over on different schedules, so MY2007 is genuinely ambiguous. The V35 sedan ran MY2003-2006 and the V35 coupe ran MY2003-2007; the V36 sedan arrived for MY2007 and kept the G35 badge through MY2008. Therefore a MY2007 'G35' record is a V35 coupe OR a V36 sedan and must be disambiguated by body style (or VIN) before assignment. The V36 coupe was never a G35 — it launched for MY2008 as the G37 — and the sedan became G37 for MY2009, so complaints after MY2008 will be under the separate G37 nameplate. G35x is the AWD sedan variant (2004-2008), not a separate generation. Both generations share the Nissan FM platform with the Z (Z33/Z34).

engines: 3.5L VQ35DE V6 (260 hp early sedan automatic, 280 hp coupe, up to 298 hp in 2005-2006 6MT 'rev-up' cars)

known_issues.description: High oil consumption and blow-by from worn piston ring sealing, typically surfacing around 60,000-80,000 miles on the earliest cars.
Premature wear of the timing chain rail guides and tensioner causes rattle/tapping; disintegrating guide material can fall into the oil pan and block pickup.
Position sensor failures cause stalling at idle and no-start conditions; failure rates were high enough that Nissan addressed them through a recall/service campaign.
Rotor warping and rapid pad wear generate heavy vibration complaints, concentrated on the sedan in the early years.
TCC solenoid failure as early as around 30,000 miles causes slippage and hard shifts; the fix pairs solenoid replacement with a PCM reflash per TSB.
Chain guide/tensioner wear producing rattle continues to be reported into the VQ35HR years.

So MY2012-2014 'Impreza' records may be either a 4th-gen economy car or a 3rd-gen WRX/STI, and must be split by trim/VIN. known_issues.description: Internal head gasket failure on the 2.5L DOHC EJ25D — combustion gases into the cooling system and coolant into the cylinders, causing overheating and misfire.
External head gasket seepage on the SOHC 2.5L: oil and/or coolant weeping at the head-to-block joint, typically on the passenger side.
External head gasket oil/coolant seepage continues on the naturally aspirated 2.5L; Subaru's interim fix was a cooling-system conditioner, with gasket replacement as the durable repair.
The banjo-bolt oil feed filter to the turbo clogs with oil coking and debris, starving the turbo bearing and causing turbo failure that can send debris downstream into the engine.

generations.platform_code: GE/GH (narrow body sedan/hatch); GR/GV (wide body WRX/STI)

known_issues.description: Head gasket seepage remains a reported wear item on the naturally aspirated EJ 2.5L in the early years of this generation.

Defective piston rings allow excessive oil consumption between changes. A class action covering FB-engine Subarus (Forester, Outback, Crosstrek, Impreza, Legacy, roughly MY2011-2015) settled with warranty extension to 8 years/100,000 miles for oil-consumption repairs plus reimbursement; the Impreza classes were 2012-2013 4-door and 5-door and 2012-2015 manual-transmission cars below specified VIN breaks.
Chain/pulley and valve body complaints (shudder, hesitation, failure) led Subaru to extend CVT powertrain coverage to 10 years/100,000 miles on CVT-equipped vehicles from the 2010-2015 model years.

The aluminum positive crankcase ventilation valve can come apart, allowing the separated pieces to be drawn into the engine and cause loss of power while driving. Subaru recalls WUP-01 (2017-2018 Impreza and 2018 Crosstrek) and WUS-04 (2017 Impreza) provide inspection/replacement, with engine replacement if the separated pieces cannot be found.

engines: 2.0L FB20 flat-4 (152 hp, Base and Sport)

notes: NHTSA span 1996-2005 falls entirely inside the 4th and 5th generations; earlier generations (1973-75, 1978-80, 1985-91) are out of scope and omitted. Both in-scope generations are GM N-body FWD compacts built at Lansing, MI. The 5th gen shares its GMX130 architecture and nearly all mechanicals with the Oldsmobile Alero — complaint patterns should correlate strongly between the two pages. MY2005 was a truncated model year: production ended 10 May 2005 and 2005 Grand Ams were a small, mostly fleet SE run, so 2005 complaint counts will be thin. Sources broadly agree on the 1998/1999 boundary; no dispute found.

known_issues.description: 3.1L V6 lower intake manifold gasket degradation, allowing coolant into the crankcase and/or external coolant seepage; associated with Dex-Cool long-life coolant and the nylon-carrier/silicone gasket design used across GM 3.1L/3.4L 60-degree V6s. Subject of the GM Dex-Cool class action covering roughly 1995-2003 3.1L/3.4L vehicles.
2.4L LD9 Twin Cam head gasket failure, often secondary to cooling-system neglect or overheating; also timing chain tensioner wear producing cold-start rattle.
Passlock/VATS theft-deterrent system faults cause intermittent crank-no-start with the security lamp lit; the fix is typically the ignition lock cylinder housing sensor rather than the engine.
Power window regulator cable/pulley failure, most often the front doors.

3.4L LA1 V6 lower intake manifold gasket failure: the gasket carrier and sealing beads deteriorate, letting coolant into the lifter valley and oil, or leaking externally at the head-to-block junction. Frequently escalates to overheating and secondary head gasket failure if not caught. Same failure family as the GM Dex-Cool 3.1L/3.4L class action.
2.4L LD9 head gasket failure and coolant loss; the LD9 was dropped after 2001 in favor of the 2.2L Ecotec.
Passlock II theft-deterrent no-start: the ignition-cylinder Hall-effect sensor degrades, the BCM disables fuel, and the car cranks but will not start until a 10-30 minute relearn.
Front rotor thickness variation / warping producing pedal pulsation, a high-frequency owner complaint on this platform.

notes: Single generation only — the Alero existed for model years 1999-2004 and nothing else wore the nameplate. Production ran April 1998 to 29 April 2004; the Alero was the final Oldsmobile ever built. Mechanically it is the Pontiac Grand Am 5th generation with different sheetmetal and interior, so its failure-mode profile is essentially identical (3.4L LA1 intake gaskets, Passlock, window regulators). If the site cross-links generations, Alero 1999-2004 and Grand Am 1999-2005 should point at each other. NHTSA span 1999-2004 matches the generation exactly.

known_issues.description: 3.4L LA1 lower intake manifold gasket failure allowing coolant into the oil or external coolant leaks; tied to the Dex-Cool-era nylon/silicone gasket design shared across GM 3.1L/3.4L 60-degree V6s. Often precedes overheating and head gasket damage.
Passlock II ignition-cylinder sensor degradation causing intermittent crank-no-start with security lamp.
Blower motor resistor / control failure leaving the fan stuck on one speed or dead.

notes: US-market mapping. The LaCrosse was sold in Canada as the Buick Allure for MY2005-2009 to avoid a French-language trademark conflict, and continued in China well past 2019 on a separate cadence — neither affects US NHTSA data. North American production ended 15 February 2019, so MY2019 is the last US year and the NHTSA 2005-2019 span is fully covered with no gaps. Note the 3rd-gen transmission progression is the one detail where secondary sources vary: MY2017 V6 cars use the 8-speed 8L45, while MY2018-2019 moved to a 9-speed (9T50 family); treat any 2017 9-speed attribution as suspect.

known_issues.description: 3.6L LY7 DOHC V6 timing chain stretch from wear on the chains, guides and tensioners, setting P0008/P0009/P0011/P0016 correlation codes with a cold-start rattle; aggravated by extended oil change intervals. GM issued TSBs and special coverage on the 3.6L family.
4T65-E 4-speed automatic pressure-control solenoid and 3-4 clutch wear causing harsh or delayed shifts, particularly on higher-torque 3.6L and 5.3L applications.
3.8L Series III V6 upper/lower intake and plenum sealing leaks are a lower-frequency issue than on earlier GM 3.1L/3.4L V6s; the Series III is generally the durable choice in this generation.

engines: 2.4L LAF Ecotec I4 with eAssist mild hybrid (2012-2016; 2.4L non-eAssist 2011)

known_issues.description: 3.6L LLT timing chain stretch. Root cause chain: internal oil consumption (early valve cover / PCV design) combined with an oil life monitor that did not account for the consumption, so the engine ran low on oil and starved the chain tensioners. Presents as cold-start rattle plus P0008/P0009/P0011/P0016. GM Special Coverage Adjustment #11340 extended timing chain coverage to 10 years / 120,000 miles. The 2012 switch to the LFX revised the chain hardware and largely resolved it.
2.4L LAF Ecotec excessive oil consumption attributed to piston ring and PCV design, which can in turn starve the variable valve timing actuators (P0011/P0014).
eAssist 115V lithium-ion battery pack and power-inverter module failures, and accessory-belt-driven motor/generator faults, disabling stop-start and electric assist.
9-speed automatic (9T50 family) harsh or delayed shifts and low-speed shudder reported after the 2018 changeover; GM issued fluid and control-module reprogramming bulletins for the 9-speed family.
Auto stop-start restart hesitation and starter/battery-management complaints, common to the LGX and LKW stop-start applications.

notes: IMPORTANT — there is a real two-year US model-year gap: no 2013 or 2014 Chevrolet Colorado was sold in North America. First-gen production ended August 2012 and the second generation launched as a MY2015 truck (many built in calendar 2014 but titled as 2015s). Do not bridge 2012-2015 into one page. The GMC Canyon is the badge-engineered twin across all three generations and shares every listed defect. NHTSA span 2004-2025 is covered by gens 1-3 plus the recorded gap; a handful of complaints keyed to 2013/2014 would be data errors.

known_issues.description: Intake valve seat and valve guide wear on the Atlas I4/I5 engines. Worn guides destroy the valve stem seals, oil is drawn past the guides, and the valve seats then recess or leak, producing combustion leakage, misfire and a Service Engine Soon lamp. GM extended coverage to 7 years / 100,000 miles for the affected early trucks. 2004-2006 units are materially worse than 2007-2008.
Excessive oil consumption on the 3.5L/3.7L I5, linked to the valve guide/seal wear above plus high crankcase pressure and PCV system failure that pulls oil into the intake tract and airbox.
Sensing and Diagnostic Module fault that can prevent frontal airbag and seat-belt pretensioner deployment; covered by a GM safety recall spanning the generation.
Blend door actuator failure producing stuck temperature control and clicking behind the dash.

8L45/8L90 8-speed torque converter shudder and harsh 2-3 / 3-4 shifts. Mechanism: the original Dexron-HP fluid degrades and the torque converter clutch chatters at light throttle around 25-50 mph. GM's remedy was a fluid flush to the revised Mobil 1 Dexron-HP specification plus control module reprogramming, and the issue is the subject of consumer litigation across GM's 8-speed applications.
2.8L LWN Duramax NOx sensor, EGR and DEF-system faults triggering limp mode and reduced-power warnings.
3.6L LFX/LGZ timing chain and VVT-related codes at higher mileage, materially less frequent than on the earlier LY7/LLT versions of the 3.6L.

engines: 2.7L L3B turbo I4 (310 hp, and 310 hp/430 lb-ft high-output)

known_issues.description: Too recent for a well-established systemic failure pattern; complaint volume is dominated by early-build electrical/infotainment concerns rather than a documented mechanical defect mechanism. Avoid asserting a named failure mode for this generation without further data.

notes: NHTSA 'YUKON' bundles the short-wheelbase Yukon, the long-wheelbase Yukon XL and the Denali trims; this map follows the mainstream short-wheelbase Yukon. Two naming/boundary traps: (1) the Yukon XL name only begins with MY2000 — before that the long-wheelbase GMC was called Suburban, so pre-2000 Yukon XL records should not exist; (2) the Yukon Denali, introduced for MY1999, stayed on the old GMT400 platform for MY2000 even though every other Yukon moved to GMT800 that year, so a MY2000 Denali is a first-generation vehicle while a MY2000 Yukon SLT is a second-generation vehicle. The GMT400 4-door Yukon began MY1995; the 2-door began MY1992. Chevrolet Tahoe/Suburban and Cadillac Escalade are the mechanical twins throughout.

known_issues.description: Central Sequential Fuel Injection (CSFI) 'spider' injector assembly on the Vortec 5.7L: the poppet-valve nozzles and pressure regulator leak internally, causing hard starting, rough idle, misfire and raw fuel odor. GM's later fix was the MFI conversion kit with individual injectors.
4L60-E 3-4 clutch pack and sun shell failure producing loss of 3rd/4th or flare shifts, especially in towing use.
Kelsey-Hayes EBCM / wheel speed sensor faults causing ABS activation at low speed and extended stopping distance; steel brake line corrosion in road-salt states.

Instrument cluster gauge stepper motor failure: needles read incorrectly, stick, or die entirely — speedometer and fuel gauge most often. GM offered extended coverage on the affected clusters. Earlier 1999-2002 clusters use air-core movements and fail less often than the 2003-2006 stepper-motor units.
Early-production 4.8L/5.3L plastic lower intake manifold and gasket seepage allowing coolant into the oil.
Intermediate steering shaft wear producing a clunk or knock felt through the wheel on turn-in; addressed by GM bulletins and a redesigned shaft.
4L60-E/4L65-E harsh shifting from a cracked 1-2 accumulator piston, and 3-4 clutch wear.

engines: 5.3L LMG/LC9/LY5 V8 with Active Fuel Management

known_issues.description: Generation IV 5.3L LC9 excessive oil consumption. Mechanism: low-tension piston oil control rings plus the Active Fuel Management oil pressure relief valve spraying oil at the cylinder walls during 4-cylinder operation, leading to oil burning, spark plug fouling and eventual internal wear. Settled US class action covering the 2011-2014 Yukon, Yukon XL, Tahoe, Suburban, Silverado, Sierra and Avalanche.
AFM lifter collapse: a deactivating lifter fails to re-latch, bending the pushrod and damaging the camshaft lobe; presents as a misfire on one cylinder plus ticking.
Widely reported dashboard top-pad cracking and splitting, generally around the passenger airbag seam.

engines: 5.3L L83 EcoTec3 V8 (355 hp, DI + AFM)

known_issues.description: Active Fuel Management lifter failure on the L83/L86: a collapsed deactivating lifter bends its pushrod and wipes the camshaft lobe, causing misfire, ticking and in severe cases full engine replacement. Subject of ongoing consumer litigation covering 2014-2020 Yukon, Yukon XL, Tahoe, Suburban, Silverado, Sierra and Escalade.

8L90 8-speed torque converter clutch shudder and harsh shifting caused by degradation of the original transmission fluid; GM's remedy was a flush to the revised Mobil 1 Dexron-HP fluid plus reprogramming, with extended coverage on affected units.

6.2L L87 V8 connecting rod and crankshaft main bearing failure. Mechanism per GM's own filing: manufacturing defects including machining sediment left in oil passages and out-of-specification crankshaft/rod components, causing bearing wear, knocking and sudden loss of propulsion. NHTSA recall 25V-274 (April 2025) covered roughly 597,000 2021-2024 Yukon, Yukon XL, Tahoe, Suburban, Silverado 1500, Sierra 1500 and Escalade. NHTSA ODI opened an engineering analysis in October 2025 after 1,157 bearing-failure reports, including 173 on vehicles outside the recall population, and is reviewing whether the recall remedy is effective.
known_issues.affected_years: 2021-2024 (6.2L L87); investigation extends to adjacent years

known_issues.description: Dynamic Fuel Management lifter failure on the L84/L87, the successor pattern to the earlier AFM lifter problem.
Air ride / adaptive damping module and compressor faults on the independent rear suspension models, new to this generation.

notes: US-market mapping. The CX-9 was a North America-first model, so there is no meaningful US-vs-global split. First-generation US model years are 2007-2015 (there was no MY2006 in the US). known_issues.description: Internal water pump seal failure. The pump is chain-driven and located inside the timing cover, so when the seal fails coolant is dumped directly into the engine oil rather than leaking externally. There is often no visible drip and no warning until the oil is contaminated, bearings are starved and the engine is destroyed. Typically surfaces around 90,000-120,000 miles. Widely reported across the generation and the subject of owner class action activity.
Transmission control module failure on early cars causing harsh shifting, limp mode and no-start; Mazda extended warranty coverage on the TCM for the early model years.
Power transfer unit / transfer case failure on AWD models, presenting as whine, vibration and loss of drive to the rear axle.

engines: 2.5L Skyactiv-G turbo I4 (PY-VPTS), 227 hp on 87 octane / 250 hp on 93 octane

known_issues.description: Direct-injection carbon deposit accumulation on the intake valves of the 2.5L turbo, producing rough cold running and misfire at higher mileage — the generic DI pattern rather than a Mazda-specific defect.
Low-pressure fuel pump impeller cracking (Denso-supplied pumps) causing stalling and no-start; recalled across multiple Mazda models of this era.

No single dominant catastrophic failure mode comparable to the first generation's water pump; complaint density is materially lower. The V6-to-turbo-four change means first-generation failure modes should not be carried forward to this page.

Critical: there is a two-model-year US gap — no Sportage was sold in the United States for MY2003 or MY2004, because Kia dropped the body-on-frame first generation after MY2002 and did not launch the unibody second generation until MY2005. Do not bridge 2002-2005. Global first-generation production continued to 2005 in other markets; the US end date is 2002. US launch years also lag the global debut by roughly one year for every generation (SL: global 2010, US MY2011; QL: global 2015, US MY2017; NQ5: global 2021, US MY2023). The first generation is a completely different kind of vehicle from everything after it — body-on-frame with a Mazda engine — so its page should not be merged with any later one.

engines: 2.0L Mazda FE DOHC I4 (SOHC in early cars)

known_issues.description: 2.0L FE timing belt is a scheduled replacement item; neglect causes belt failure. Documentation of a distinct systemic defect mechanism for this generation is thin compared with later ones — treat complaint clusters cautiously.
Frame and body corrosion in road-salt states on the body-on-frame chassis.

known_issues.description: Occupant classification system and airbag-control-unit recalls affecting this platform generation.
Pre-GDI Beta II and Delta engines; this generation predates the Theta II direct-injection bearing failures and should not be tagged with them.

known_issues.description: Theta II GDI connecting rod bearing failure. Mechanism: metallic debris left in the engine block oil galleries during machining restricts oil flow to the rod bearings, which then wear and seize; presents as a deep knock, then loss of power and engine seizure, in some cases with non-crash engine-compartment fire. Kia began with a 2016 campaign on 2011-2014 Optima/Sorento/Sportage, followed by formal recalls in 2017 and later, a knock-sensor detection software campaign, and a $1.3B consolidated class settlement covering roughly 2011-2019 Hyundai and Kia models including the Sportage.
Non-crash engine-compartment fires reported on Theta II vehicles; NHTSA's investigation of Hyundai/Kia handling of these engine defects produced record civil penalties.

engines: 2.0L Theta II turbo GDI I4 (SX Turbo, 240 hp)

known_issues.description: Theta II connecting rod bearing failure claims continue into the early years of this generation; the class settlement population extends to roughly MY2019 for affected Theta II applications.

known_issues.description: Too recent for a documented systemic failure mechanism; complaints skew toward electronics and driver-assist behavior. Do not carry Theta II failure modes forward — the Smartstream engines are a different family.

notes: US-market mapping. US sales ended after MY2022; there is no MY2023+ US Accent, so the NHTSA span 1996-2022 is exactly the model's US life from the 1996 side. The Accent used port injection for most of its US life; only the fourth generation (RB) ran the 1.6L Gamma GDI direct-injection engine.

known_issues.description: 1.5L Alpha is an interference design; timing belt neglect causes valve damage. Little else is systematically documented for this generation in US sources.
Alpha II timing belt service interval; crank position sensor and ignition coil failures causing stalling are the most commonly reported items.

engines: 1.6L Alpha II CVVT G4ED I4 (110 hp)

known_issues.description: Timing belt driven engine with CVVT; belt and tensioner service is the dominant maintenance-related failure. No large-scale systemic defect campaign specific to this generation in the US.

engines: 1.6L Gamma GDI G4FD I4 (138 hp, direct injection)

known_issues.description: Anti-lock Brake System module internal brake fluid leak causing an electrical short and engine-compartment fire, which can occur while parked as well as while driving. Root cause identified as the material formulation of the ABS module O-ring rubber, which deteriorates and allows internal leakage. Hyundai Safety Recall 251 / NHTSA 23V-651 covers certain 2012-2015 Accent vehicles built 5 March 2011 to 31 October 2014; the interim remedy is an ABS fuse replacement and owners were told to park outside pending repair.
1.6L Gamma GDI intake valve carbon deposits from direct injection, causing rough idle and misfire at higher mileage; also high-pressure fuel pump tick.

IVT (chain-type CVT) introduced for MY2020 — owner complaints center on shudder, hesitation and belt/pulley behavior rather than a formally recalled defect. Note this as a mid-generation powertrain change: 2018-2019 and 2020-2022 Accents have materially different transmission failure profiles.
US sales ended after MY2022; complaint volume for this generation is low relative to the RB generation.

notes: North American mapping — this matters, because 'Frontier' elsewhere is a badge for the global NP300/Navara, and from 2022 the North American truck is a dedicated model no longer shared with the global line. Two boundary traps: (1) the second generation (D40) is unusually long, MY2005-2021, and the redesign was delayed so a full MY2021 D40 exists — do not assume 2021 is the new truck; (2) inside the D40 there is a major mid-generation powertrain change for MY2020, when the 4.0L VQ40DE and 5-speed automatic were replaced by the 3.8L VQ38DD (310 hp) and a 9-speed automatic while the old body carried over. That 2020 change resets the drivetrain failure profile mid-generation and should be surfaced on the D40 page. Nissan states 93 percent of the VQ38DD's components are new or redesigned versus the VQ40DE.

known_issues.description: KA24DE timing chain guide and tensioner wear producing a cold-start rattle and, if ignored, chain slap and guide fragmentation.
Frame and rear structure corrosion in road-salt regions, a recurring theme in owner reports across Nissan compact trucks of this era.
Exhaust manifold cracking and pre-cat material ingestion reports on the four-cylinder trucks.

The 'strawberry milkshake of death' (SMOD). The automatic transmission fluid cooler is integrated inside the radiator end tank; when the internal seal fails, engine coolant and ATF cross-mix. The fluid turns pink and foamy, the transmission slips, overheats and fails. Reported as early as roughly 60,000 miles with a cluster around 110,000. The only durable fix is a radiator with an external cooler plus transmission replacement. A nationwide class action filed in 2010 covering the Frontier, Xterra and Pathfinder produced a settlement in 2013; the associated warranty extensions have expired.
known_issues.affected_years: 2005-2010 automatics (most heavily documented); risk persists on later radiators of the same design

known_issues.description: VQ40DE timing chain guide and tensioner wear causing rattle at start-up and, in advanced cases, cam timing codes.

Not a defect, but essential for grouping: MY2020-2021 D40 trucks use the VQ38DD and the Jatco JR913E 9-speed. Complaints on 2020-2021 units concern the new powertrain and share nothing mechanically with the 2005-2019 VQ40DE/RE5R05A failure modes above.
Frame corrosion reports in salt-belt states across the long production run.

Too recent for an established systemic failure mechanism. Received a mid-cycle refresh for MY2025 (new 12.3-inch infotainment, revised styling, tow rating to 7,150 lb), so 2025-and-later complaints may skew toward the new electronics rather than the carryover powertrain.

notes: US-market mapping; the Avalon was primarily a North America model so there is little US-vs-global divergence (the Japanese-market Avalon was a short-lived early variant, and later Chinese/Australian derivatives do not affect NHTSA data). The XX50 is the first Avalon on the TNGA-K architecture and the first to offer AWD (2021-2022, four-cylinder only).

known_issues.description: 1MZ-FE V6 oil gelling/sludge. Engines built roughly 1997-2002 are the affected population; restricted oil return and PCV design combined with extended oil change intervals allow sludge to block oil passages and destroy bearings. Toyota settled a class action in 2007 covering an estimated 2-5 million 1997-2002 Toyota and Lexus vehicles, providing repair coverage for 8 years from purchase.
Continuation of the 1MZ-FE sludge population; the settled class covers engines built through 2002, so MY2000-2002 Avalons are inside it and MY2003-2004 generally are not.
Driver's power window master switch and combination-switch failures are a common owner-reported item on this generation.

2GR-FE rubber oil supply hose feeding the VVT-i controller can rupture, causing rapid loss of engine oil and possible engine damage or fire; Toyota recalled affected 2GR-FE vehicles and replaced the rubber section with a metal line.
Included in Toyota's 2009-2010 floor mat pedal entrapment recalls covering unintended acceleration risk on several 2005-2010 models.
